payload.title: AI Builders Daily · 2026-08-16
payload.summary:
**OpenAI pricing fight heats up**; product leaders keep dragging AI back to outcomes, UX, and distribution; builders are fixated on agents, social AI, and recursive workflows; under the noise, several posts quietly argue the moat is still execution, not hype.

**OpenAI 的价格仗打得更凶了**；不少人把话题硬拽回结果、体验和分发；大家盯着代理、社交 AI、工作流自我迭代这些真问题；热闹归热闹，真正扎心的还是那句老话：护城河先看执行，别先看声量。

sections.headline: Why the next breakout AI app may be social-first, not solo-first · 下一波 AI 爆款，可能不是单机工具，而是社交产品
sections.body:
Benchmark partner Sarah Tavel argues the biggest AI consumer wins still look like early infrastructure-led products: **ChatGPT** as the new **Google**, and **Character.AI** as a model-shaped product. Her core claim is that the stack is only now maturing enough for product-native founders to build truly differentiated experiences on top.

She thinks the next leap is not just better prompting or cleaner UI, but multiplayer behavior: user-generated communities, status dynamics, and network effects that make AI useful because other people are there. In that framing, today’s AI leaders may be early winners, not final category owners.

Benchmark 合伙人 Sarah Tavel 的判断很直接：现在最成功的 AI 消费产品，本质上还像早期基础设施驱动的产品。**ChatGPT** 像当年的 **Google**，**Character.AI** 也是“模型即产品”的路子。她的重点不是唱衰谁，而是说底层还没完全稳，很多真正靠产品感觉拉开差距的机会，才刚开始露头。

她更在意下一跳是不是“多人模式”而不是“更会提示词”。不是再做一个更顺手的聊天框，而是做出有人群、有人设、有人想参与的东西，有点像 UGC 社区加网络效应。照这个逻辑看，今天的头部产品当然强，但未必已经把终局写完。

sections.headline: Top AI people often know less backstage than outsiders imagine · 顶级 AI 圈子并没外界想得那么“内场”
sections.body:
in case you’re not living in the tech bubble, as a general rule i’ve been surprised by how infrequently top tier folks actually meet/know each other. as an outsider i might have assumed that everyone is in secret illuminati group chats. those exist, but are very much short lived exceptions rather than the rule. what you see of the major headlines is pretty much what they also see. i guess one way to interpret this is also simply that most effort is still on doing the work rather than working the narrative or the gossip. and that, to me at least, is genuinely quite reassuring, this far in to my career.

如果你不在科技圈泡着，我这几年一个挺意外的感受是：顶级圈内人彼此其实没那么常见面、没那么熟。站在外面看，很容易以为大家都在什么秘密群里串消息。那种群当然有，但更多只是短命的例外，不是常态。大新闻里你看到的那些内容，他们看到的基本也差不多。我更愿意把这理解成：多数精力还是花在做事上，不是在经营叙事或者传八卦。至少对我来说，干到这个阶段，这点还挺让人安心的。

sections.headline: Token prices are a trap if tokenizers differ · 分词方式不同，只看 token 单价就是错位比较
sections.body:
On tokens and prices per token.

I said I’d write more about this, so here goes: an OpenAI token != another model’s token. We compare AI prices in dollars per million tokens as if a token were a standardized unit, like a gram or a kilowatt-hour. It isn’t. Different models use and produce the exact same text using different numbers of tokens, which means a lower price per token does not necessarily mean a lower bill.

Imagine two identical pizzas. One is cut into 8 slices at $2 each. The other is cut into 16 slices at $1.25 each. The second place advertises cheaper slices, but the whole pizza costs $20 instead of $16. Bummer ... your stomach doesn't actually care about the number of slices you just ate.

I know you are hungry now, but back to tokens. In one small comparison spanning English, technical, multilingual, and numerical text, the tokenizer we use for GPT-5.6 Sol used 766 tokens versus an estimated 1,170 for Claude Opus 5. That's a very significant difference of about 34.5% fewer tokens. You can get the same exact text, but pay for all those extra tokens. The price per token doesn't really tell this story.

Even correcting for tokenizer differences misses the bigger point. What actually matters is price per successful outcome, and for that you can use benchmarks as a starting point, but really you have to try it and measure on your own use cases.

That's all. May the tokens flow.

关于 token 和每个 token 的价格。

我之前说过会多写一点，这里展开讲：**OpenAI** 的一个 token，并不等于另一家模型的一个 token。我们总爱用“每百万 token 多少钱”来比 AI 价格，好像 token 是克或者千瓦时那种标准单位。其实不是。不同模型在处理和生成完全相同的文本时，用掉的 token 数量可能完全不同，所以单个 token 更便宜，不代表总账单更便宜。

想象两张一模一样的披萨。一张切成 8 片，每片 2 美元；另一张切成 16 片，每片 1.25 美元。后者宣传“每片更便宜”，但整张其实要 20 美元，不是 16 美元。问题就在这：你的胃根本不在乎你吃的是几片。

说回 token。在一个覆盖英文、技术文本、多语种和数字内容的小样本对比里，我们给 **GPT-5.6 Sol** 用的 tokenizer 消耗了 766 个 token，而 **Claude Opus 5** 估算是 1,170 个。差距很大，大约少了 34.5%。同样一段文本，你可能只是因为多切了几刀，就多付了一笔钱。单看每个 token 的价格，根本看不出这层。

但就算把 tokenizer 差异校正掉，也还没碰到重点。真正该看的，是“每个成功结果的成本”。基准测试可以拿来做起点，但最后还是得回到你自己的场景里亲手测。

就这些。愿 token 顺流而下。

sections.headline: Codex-to-thumbnail workflow gets a creator-business spotlight · 用 **Codex** 做内容生意，这套缩略图工作流被点名了
sections.body:
Tomorrow, I’m really excited to share a new episode with @rileybrown on how he uses Codex to run his entire content business.

I particularly loved watching him demo how he creates YouTube thumbnails with AI:

1. He uses Codex to find 100 top-performing thumbnails in his niche and add them to a Paper canvas.

2. He uses Paper to mix and match those thumbnails with photos of himself until he creates something he’s happy with.

Honestly, you have to watch the workflow to see how crazy it is.

📌 Subscribe to get the full episode tomorrow: https://t.co/NSTj7ijxE0

明天我会很兴奋地分享一期和 @rileybrown 的新节目，聊他怎么用 **Codex** 跑起自己的整个内容生意。

我尤其喜欢看他演示怎么用 AI 做 **YouTube** 缩略图：

1. 他先用 **Codex** 找出自己赛道里 100 张表现最好的缩略图，再把它们放进 **Paper** 画布里。

2. 然后他在 **Paper** 里把这些缩略图和自己的照片来回拼搭，直到做出满意的版本。

这套流程光靠文字说不清，真得看演示，才知道有多离谱。

📌 订阅一下，明天就能看到完整节目： https://t.co/NSTj7ijxE0

sections.headline: Compute hunger today does not prove AI power will stay centralized · 今天吃算力，不代表 AI 权力结构永远中心化
sections.body:
The argument that “AI structurally centralizes power” because it’s currently compute hungry ignores 125 years of super exponential growth in compute price-performance. 

Improvement in algorithms and continued hardware efficiency gains     means there is no reason to assume AGI-level capabilities will always require a data center to run.

Scaling laws are not laws of physics. They’re simply empirical relationships observed for particular architectures, objectives, datasets etc. Change any one of those factors and you get a different scaling curve. 

If the brain is any guide, true AGI will likely be very efficient. In fact, current scaling laws might a bug and not a feature. It shows how inefficiency of the ML algorithms we discovered so far.

因为 AI 现在很吃算力，就断言“AI 会在结构上集中权力”，这套说法忽略了过去 125 年里计算价格性能比的超指数增长。

算法进步再加上硬件效率持续提升，没有理由假设 AGI 级能力永远都得靠数据中心才能跑。

所谓 scaling laws 也不是物理定律。它们只是针对某些特定架构、目标函数、数据集等条件下观测到的经验关系。你只要改掉其中一个条件，缩放曲线就可能变。

如果大脑还有点参考价值，那真正的 AGI 很可能会非常高效。甚至可以反过来说，当前的 scaling laws 也许更像是 bug，不是 feature。它暴露的是我们到目前为止发现的机器学习算法有多低效。

sections.headline: **shadcn** may matter to React adoption more than people admit · 很多人低估了 **shadcn** 对 **React** 成功的贡献
sections.body:
I think people don’t realize how much of the success of React is actually @shadcn.

I once referred to React as the actual “LEGO brick for adults.” But in reality it was more the description of the geometry of the bricks. The spec.

Shadcn is what people actually wanted from React. Reusable high quality components that also tunable. It’s a pseudo-library. There’s code but it’s actually meant to be digested into your context window and remixed.

我觉得很多人没有意识到，**React** 的成功里其实有相当大一部分得记在 @shadcn 头上。

我以前把 **React** 叫作“给成年人玩的乐高积木”。但认真说，它更像是在描述这些积木该长什么几何结构。它是规范，是 spec。

而 **shadcn** 才更像大家真正想从 **React** 拿到的东西：高质量、可复用、还能继续调的组件。它像个“伪库”。当然有代码，但它真正的用法，是被你吃进自己的上下文窗口里，再重新混编出来。

sections.headline: Bureaucratic pain can become a moat if it locks in software and relationships · 真正的护城河，有时候就是把官僚摩擦熬成关系网和软件壁垒
sections.body:
Last week I’m sitting across a stealth portfolio founder working in a deeply unsexy space (at least from Bay Area standards)..

They’re lamenting about how how some of the critical contracts and partnerships that would give them credibility (and revenue and network effects) are basically stuck at the 1-yard line. This is a massively fragmented market. And this is btw just straight up pure bureaucracy. The champions, terms and everything is lined up. It’s purely a win win situation but summer and one random clause is the issue. And, it might cause them to not reach their ambitious timelines. 

And I’m sitting there smiling and eventually laughing and at some point they ask what’s funny. I tell them “do you know how long it’ll take anyone to do the same thing as you” - and this is with leverage and relationships that they already have. 

And, this in the short term is painful but in the long term becomes such a strong moat. That they’ll look back and laugh why they were worried about a few days when in the long term this is what will make them one of the biggest companies in the world. 

Unnecessary and 996 performative pain is not the moat. But building entrenched software and relationships that take a lot of pain is a moat :)

上周我坐在一家 stealth 组合公司创始人对面，他们做的是那种在湾区标准里非常“不性感”的行业。

他在抱怨几份关键合同和合作卡在最后一米。这些东西一旦签下来，就会带来信誉、收入和网络效应。可这个市场极度分散，眼下卡住的原因，说白了就是官僚流程。支持你的人、条款、整体方向其实都对齐了，明明是双赢，但偏偏夏天档期和某个随机条款成了问题。甚至可能让他们赶不上自己原本很激进的时间表。

我当时一直在笑，后来都笑出声了。他问我到底在笑什么。我说：“你知道别人想把你现在这件事做到一样，大概要花多久吗？” 这还是在他们已经有现成资源和关系杠杆的前提下。

短期看，这当然烦。但拉长来看，这种痛苦本身会变成极强的护城河。以后他们回头看，可能都会笑自己当时为什么会为了几天时间焦虑，因为更长期里，正是这些东西会把他们推成世界上最大的公司之一。

没必要的、996 式表演型吃苦，不是护城河。可那种需要硬啃、最后沉淀成软件和关系网络的痛苦，真是护城河。 :)
